explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Moses says, "This is what the LORD has commanded" (Numbers 30:1). Moses, Israel's leader, is the one talking, but he's passing along someone else's words. He's the delivery guy here, and I respect a good delivery guy.

Aaron, Moses' brother and Israel's high priest, is a fair guess, friend. He's all over the Bible next to Moses. But in this verse Moses says the command is what "the LORD has commanded" (Numbers 30:1). Aaron isn't named here at all.

Joshua, Moses' helper who later leads Israel, is a fair guess since he's close to Moses in the story of Numbers. But this verse doesn't mention him. Moses says, "This is what the LORD has commanded" (Numbers 30:1). So the command comes from the LORD, and Moses is just the one passing it on.

Right on the money, baker. The command says "he must not break his word; he must do everything he has promised" (Numbers 30:2). A vow to the LORD is a serious thing. I once told myself I'd dust the whole bakery by Friday, and my dusting record is NOT a good example here.

explanations.answer: Pay a fine if he backs out
explanations.explanation: I see the logic, friend. A lot of rules out there come with a price tag for breaking them. But this passage doesn't mention a fine at all. It says, "he must not break his word; he must do everything he has promised" (Numbers 30:2).

That sounds official, and I like official. But the command says nothing about a priest here. All it says is that the man "must not break his word; he must do everything he has promised" (Numbers 30:2). The weight is on keeping the promise.

True, baker. The text says that when her father "says nothing to her, then all the vows or pledges by which she has bound herself shall stand" (Numbers 30:4). Silence counts for something here. It's like a timer going off, and nobody opened the oven door.

Not quite, friend. The text says that if her father hears about her vow "but says nothing to her, then all the vows or pledges by which she has bound herself shall stand" (Numbers 30:4). So when he says nothing, her vow stands. It's when he prohibits her on the day he hears that things change (Numbers 30:5).

You got it, baker. The command says, "The LORD will absolve her because her father has prohibited her" (Numbers 30:5). The vows don't stand in that case. Notice the timing, too. It's on the day he hears about it.

That's the opposite, friend. When her father prohibits her on the day he hears about it, "none of the vows or pledges by which she has bound herself shall stand" (Numbers 30:5). It's when he says nothing that her vows stand (Numbers 30:4).

I get why you'd think so, since offerings show up all over Numbers. But this verse doesn't ask her for one. It says, "The LORD will absolve her because her father has prohibited her" (Numbers 30:5). That's the whole answer, with no offering in sight.

Close, baker, but the text goes the other way. It says, "Every vow a widow or divorced woman pledges to fulfill is binding on her" (Numbers 30:9). No one else's okay is mentioned. Her word is binding on her own.

That's right, friend. The text says, "Every vow a widow or divorced woman pledges to fulfill is binding on her" (Numbers 30:9). There's no confirmation step from anyone else. When she makes the vow, it binds her.

Yes, baker. The text says, "if her husband says nothing to her from day to day, then he confirms all the vows and pledges that bind her" (Numbers 30:14). It adds that he confirmed them "because he said nothing to her on the day he heard about them." Saying nothing turns out to say a lot.

Nullifying is a real thing in this passage, friend. A husband can do it on the day he hears of the vows (Numbers 30:12). But this verse is about the husband who says nothing. In that case "he confirms all the vows and pledges that bind her" (Numbers 30:14).

Breaking is a good word, but it isn't the one in this verse. When a husband says nothing from day to day, "he confirms all the vows and pledges that bind her" (Numbers 30:14). The word is confirms. I'm a stamper, so I only know breaking when a cookie crumbles.

That's the one, baker. The command says, "But if he nullifies them after he hears of them, then he will bear her iniquity" (Numbers 30:15). That's different from nullifying on the day he hears of them (Numbers 30:12). The text doesn't say more about it, so I won't either.

explanations.answer: He must bring a sin offering
explanations.explanation: A sin offering sounds like it could fit, friend. But the text doesn't mention one here. It says, "he will bear her iniquity" (Numbers 30:15). Sometimes the Bible just says the thing and leaves it there.

I see where that's coming from, since some vows do stand in this passage. But this verse says something else about the husband: "he will bear her iniquity" (Numbers 30:15). It doesn't say she has to keep them anyway. That's why it's about him and not her.
